item.title: Kim Kardashian Recalls Fearing Her Career Was Over After All’s Fair Reviews
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Kim Kardashian says brutal All's Fair reviews briefly made her fear for her career before the cast chose to double down.
item.content:encoded:
Kim Kardashian admitted the first wave of All’s Fair reviews rattled her enough to wonder if she had damaged her acting career for good.

The reality star and entrepreneur is back as divorce lawyer Allura Grant in the Hulu drama’s second season. She said the harsh response to season one briefly left her worried that her veteran co-stars would blame her for the backlash.

“There was a second when I thought, ‘Oh my God, my career is over,'” Kardashian said while promoting the new season.

That fear did not last. Kardashian said Sarah Paulson left her a supportive voicemail that restored her confidence. Her answer after hearing it was simple: “Okay, what do I do? We double down.”

The first season earned a brutal response from critics, but viewers kept watching. The attention helped All’s Fair hold a top spot on Hulu before the series secured a second-season renewal.

That split became part of the show’s story. Critics gave season one a 6 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes. The audience still pushed the series to the top of Hulu’s chart. Kardashian now sees that gap as proof that reviews did not get the final word.

Kardashian also struck a modest note during an appearance on The View.

She said creator Ryan Murphy was “setting me up for success by surrounding me with the best of the best actors.” Naomi Watts rejected the idea that Kardashian hid behind the cast, while Niecy Nash-Betts told her, “You brought your A-game, baby!”

Season two brings back Glenn Close, Paulson, Watts, Teyana Taylor and Nash-Betts. The first three episodes began streaming on Hulu this week, with new installments set to arrive weekly.

Paulson said Kardashian reached another level late in the new season. She pointed to more confidence and humor in the performance. Watts also said Kardashian grew on set and started adding her own lines. Their comments gave Kardashian an answer to the idea that she was only leaning on the ensemble.

The show is even making room for Kardashian to laugh at herself. A new scene has Allura admit she failed the bar exam on her first try, a nod to Kardashian’s own legal path. Kardashian retook California’s bar exam in July after falling short in 2025.

For now, Kardashian is answering the worst reviews of her acting career with another season, a bigger swing and the backing of the women beside her.

item.title: B2K Reunites For First Album In Nearly 24 Years With””ECLIPSE”
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: B2K reunites for ECLIPSE, the group's first studio album in nearly 24 years, with all four original members back together.
item.content:encoded:
B2K has reunited its original lineup for ECLIPSE, the group’s first studio album in nearly 24 years.

Omarion, J-Boog, Lil’ Fizz and Raz-B released the project through BPC Music Group on Friday. The group announced the album alongside the new single “Co-Sign,” which was written and produced by The Underdogs.

Raz-B framed the return as more than a nostalgia play.

“ECLIPSE is a celebration of our brotherhood, growth, and legacy. 25 years later, we’re still making history,” he said.

Omarion kept his own message short: “20+ years later, the stars have aligned.”

The album brings together a wide production team, including Sean Garrett, Troy Taylor, Hitmaka, Blaq Tuxedo, Lil Ronnie, Kenneth “KP” Paige, Ethos and The Underdogs. Eric Bellinger and Ant Clemons are among the outside songwriters credited on the project.

B2K started the rollout in July with “Mileage.” The single became the group’s first entry on Billboard’s Mainstream R&B/Hip-Hop Airplay chart in more than two decades.

It climbed to No. 23, reached the Top 15 at R&B/Hip-Hop radio and topped Apple Music’s R&B Songs and R&B Videos charts. The Atlanta bass-inspired “Lil Freak” followed in October.

The reunion has also moved beyond the studio. B2K performed new music and older hits on NBC’s TODAY before the album arrived. Earlier this year, the group’s Boys 4 Life Tour stop in Newark turned into a full reunion showcase with Bow Wow and other early-2000s acts.

ECLIPSE is the first album released by BPC Music Group, the label founded by Black Promoters Collective partners Gary Guidry and Troy Brown. The company also presented the Boys 4 Life Tour.

B2K’s last studio album, Pandemonium!, arrived in 2002. The group has seven Billboard Hot 100 entries, including the No. 1 single “Bump, Bump, Bump.” Its self-titled debut topped the R&B/Hip-Hop Albums chart and peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard 200.

The release comes after years of reunion shows, but it is the first full album from the four-man lineup since its original run.

The new album is available through major streaming services as B2K begins its first full studio chapter with all four members in more than two decades.

item.title: Macklemore Says Nine U.S. Arenas Rejected Free Palestine Tour
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: Macklemore says nine U.S. arenas rejected his Free Palestine benefit tour, but he plans to keep building shows elsewhere.
item.content:encoded:
Macklemore says nine major U.S. arenas backed away from hosting his Free Palestine benefit tour after learning what the shows were for.

According to Billboard, the Seattle rapper said he had been offered dates through the end of the year before the concerts’ purpose became clear. He named Madison Square Garden, Prudential Center, Barclays Center and UBS Arena in the New York area.

His list also included Intuit Dome, Kia Forum and Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, plus Chase Center in San Francisco and Climate Pledge Arena in Seattle.

“In over twenty years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this,” Macklemore said.

The account is Macklemore’s. He did not describe a single written policy shared by all nine buildings. Instead, he said the conversations differed but reached the same result: the proposed shows would not happen at those venues.

That distinction matters because the venues have separate owners and operators. Macklemore is alleging a pattern based on his team’s booking talks, not announcing a formal industrywide ban.

The setback comes after Macklemore completed the European leg of his Free Palestine Tour. The run opened in Dublin and continued through Paris before closing at London’s OVO Arena Wembley on October 30. The shows raised money for organizations providing medical care, food, education and other support to Palestinians.

AllHipHop previously reported that Macklemore created the benefit series after Ed Sheeran removed him from his U.S. tour.

The dispute began after the rapper called for a free Palestine during two September appearances at MetLife Stadium. Tour organizers later said venues on the route would not allow concerts to proceed with him on the bill.

Macklemore went forward with his own dates and pledged money from his Sheeran run to Palestinian aid groups. At the London finale, he told the crowd that speaking about Gaza had become easier than staying quiet.

Now the fight has shifted from what Macklemore can say onstage to whether he can secure the stages he wants. He said the U.S. benefit plans are not finished and suggested the concerts could move outside traditional arenas.

For the moment, no American dates have been announced. Macklemore says he will keep working with artists and organizers to find another way to bring the shows home.

item.title: Claressa Shields Claims She Witnessed Gervonta Davis Assault A Woman
item.dc:creator: Houston Williams
item.description: Claressa Shields escalates her feud with Gervonta Davis with an assault allegation after Papoose steps in to defend her.
item.content:encoded:
Claressa Shields has turned an unsolicited fashion critique from Gervonta Davis into a confrontation that has gotten considerably uglier than anything hanging in a closet.

Here’s how we got here. Tank mocked the outfit Claressa wore to her Atlanta music event, posting footage and telling her, “@claressashields you look a hot ass mess..” Apparently, the lightweight boxer had some heavyweight opinions about that jumpsuit. 

Papoose defended his girlfriend by mocking Davis’ performance against Lamont Roach. Davis subsequently threatened to put the rapper to sleep.

That brought a Hip-Hop relationship squarely into a boxing dispute, with everybody apparently comfortable throwing verbal punches outside their usual weight class.

Claressa also retaliated with an AI image depicting Davis wearing a version of her outfit. She accused him of selectively sharing a text exchange and made clear that neither she nor Papoose considered him a friend. The wardrobe argument had officially become personal.

Now, in the circulating remarks you shared, Shields goes considerably further:

“I know so much stuff about lil dawg, I don’t say nothing… He wanna be a girl so bad. We not gonna judge you, just come out and do it.

He’s a woman beater. Tank beat a b#### up in my face at a basketball game. I sat on that sh*t for years and never said nothing.”

Those are Shields’ allegations. Her claim that she personally witnessed an assault has not been independently established in the sources reviewed. Her comments about Davis’ gender expression also establish nothing about his identity or sexuality.

And that is where the tone changes. An outfit can inspire jokes. An allegation of violence against a woman deserves scrutiny, particularly when somebody claims to have witnessed it firsthand.

Damn, this is nasty across the board.

item.title: Pierce Freelon Joins Hip-Hop Summit Offering Students Free Mental Health And Career Workshops
item.dc:creator: AllHipHop Staff
item.description: Pierce Freelon will join Raleigh's S.M.A.S.H. Summit for a day of Hip-Hop, mental health talks and career learning for students.
item.content:encoded:
Pierce Freelon is headed to a Raleigh summit where Hip-Hop will share the bill with student mental health and career skills. The fifth annual S.M.A.S.H. Summit takes place November 7, with free admission and lunch for students.

EMPOWER ALL Inc. is organizing the event at North Carolina State University’s McKimmon Center. The program brings students into conversations about work and wellness while giving them room to make and explore art.

“Students meet mentors already working in the careers they’re curious about and hear honest conversations about wellness from people who’ve lived them,” the organization says.

Freelon’s event listing also names author Nic Stone as the keynote speaker. Interactive workshops and live performances are planned for a crowd that includes educators, artists and community partners alongside students.

The summit splits its program across Hip-Hop’s elements. MCing, DJing and breaking anchor sessions about identity, creative expression and wellness. Graffiti and knowledge provide the route into STEAM, entrepreneurship and the skills students can take into a job.

Another session preview puts Hip-Hop and spoken word poetry at the center of a discussion about healing and research. EMPOWER ALL founder Dr. Valencia Hicks Harris will join Dr. Crystal Leigh Endsley and Dr. Tony Keith Jr., with “Dear Academy” featured in the session.

Freelon brings experience teaching young people through music. He founded Blackspace in 2014 after his work with Beat Making Lab, a music education project with a global reach. Blackspace runs a digital arts studio for youth built around Afrofuturism.

Its training includes beatmaking, audio engineering, photography and videography. The organization pairs those creative skills with mentorship and work experience, giving the summit’s focus on future jobs a direct connection to Freelon’s work outside his recordings.

His recent music has focused on young listeners, too. Freelon released the children’s album Black Boy Glow on June 19. The 10-song project runs 27 minutes. Its rollout described a dedication to young Black boys, with confidence, connection and self-worth among its themes.

Doors open at 8:30 A.M., with the program running from 9 A.M. to 2 P.M. The NC State calendar lists the venue at 1101 Gorman Street in Raleigh. Student registration is available through the organizer’s ticket page.

item.title: UK Rapper Marcus La-Croix Acquitted In Teen’s 2018 Murder Case
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: UK rapper Marcus La-Croix was acquitted as the long-running Tanesha Melbourne-Blake murder case ended without convictions.
item.content:encoded:
UK rapper Marcus La-Croix was acquitted of murder and a firearms charge after a retrial over the 2018 drive-by shooting that killed 17-year-old Tanesha Melbourne-Blake in north London.

La-Croix, 38, had denied murder and possession of a firearm with intent to endanger life.

Michael Clarke, 37, faced the same charges in a separate retrial. Prosecutors offered no further evidence against Clarke on Friday, November 6, and Judge Mark Dennis KC directed jurors to return not guilty verdicts.

The decisions ended a prosecution that had moved through four trials and repeated setbacks at the Old Bailey. La-Croix’s first trial was abandoned in April 2025 after questions arose about evidence from a prison witness.

Judge Dennis said those issues needed to be “bottomed out” before the case could continue.

La-Croix was acquitted after a retrial this summer. Clarke’s second jury was discharged on October 30 after it could not reach a verdict. Judge Dennis told those jurors, “In those circumstances, I have no other option but to discharge the jury, so I discharge you.”

Tanesha was spending Easter Monday with friends on Chalgrove Road in Tottenham on April 2, 2018 when someone opened fire from a silver Vauxhall Meriva. A bullet struck her in the chest and she died at the scene. The vehicle was found burned in Barnet five days later.

Prosecutors alleged La-Croix was part of a group that traveled into rival territory before the shooting.

The case against him relied in part on a prisoner’s account of an alleged confession. La-Croix denied making that admission.

The Times reported that the first trial exposed concerns about similarities between the witness statement and an undisclosed prison intelligence report. The Metropolitan Police acknowledged disclosure failures but denied that officers had acted improperly.

Police said the gun used to kill Tanesha had also been used in the March 2018 killing of 20-year-old Joseph Williams-Torres in Walthamstow. Investigators said the weapon appeared to have circulated in north London, but they did not claim the two killings were otherwise connected.

La-Croix and Clarke were charged in July 2024, more than six years after Tanesha’s death. Both men maintained their innocence. With La-Croix acquitted and not guilty verdicts entered for Clarke, the shooting has ended without a murder conviction.

item.title: LeBron James Demands Bron AI Stop Using His Likeness In Betting Ad
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: LeBron James demanded that Bron AI stop using his likeness after a betting ad featured a lookalike and a voice resembling his own.
item.content:encoded:
LeBron James demanded that a sports betting app stop using his likeness after an ad featured a lookalike in a No. 23 jersey and a voice resembling his own.

The cease-and-desist letter targeted Bron AI, whose CEO, Anish Gupta, posted the ad on X on November 4. It showed the figure from behind as he scrolled through betting options involving athletes, Front Office Sports reported.

“LeBron is in no way affiliated with this unauthorized use of his likeness,” his spokesperson told Front Office Sports.

Lawyers at Grubman Shire Meiselas & Sacks demanded that the company stop using James’ likeness “in any manner and media.” They called the use “especially serious and egregious” and wanted every app user notified in writing that James had no involvement.

The lawyers cited his exclusive Polymarket endorsement deal and said the ad implied he bet on basketball, which NBA rules prohibit. The letter demanded an end to the promotion; the reporting did not establish that James filed a lawsuit.

Luka Dončić’s photo also appeared in the ad. His representative confirmed to Front Office Sports that he sent a cease-and-desist too. Bron AI and its owner PlayVision Inc. did not respond to the outlet’s requests for comment.

Yahoo Sports reported that the ad was removed from X.

Bron described itself as “TikTok for Sports Betting” on its Y Combinator company page. Its pitch combined recommended bets, odds comparisons and player statistics, with access to more than 150 sportsbooks and prediction markets.

It also promoted automatic bet placement. The San Francisco company was founded in 2025 by Gupta and chief technology officer Marc Zoghby and joined Y Combinator’s Fall 2025 group.

James’ media adviser Adam Mendelsohn criticized the marketing approach in comments to The Philadelphia Inquirer.

“People are all playing for the cheapest way to get clicks and aggregation. A lot of pundits do it too,” Mendelsohn said.

The dispute involved a broader concern the U.S. Copyright Office examined in its July 2024 digital replicas report: manipulated voices and images that falsely depict a person. The office recommended federal legislation after finding gaps in existing protections.

“We believe there is an urgent need for effective nationwide protection against the harms that can be caused to reputations and livelihoods,” Register of Copyrights Shira Perlmutter said when the report was released.

item.title: Kardinal Offishall Faults Canada’s Music Industry For Favoring White Pop Artists
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Kardinal Offishall said Canada's music industry gave white pop artists more support as he discussed barriers for Black artists.
item.content:encoded:
Kardinal Offishall said Canada has built more music industry support for white pop artists than Black artists, pointing to a gap he still sees after three decades in the business.

Speaking on The Brandon Gonez Show, he said there was “much more of an infrastructure for pop artists in Canada and white pop artists in Canada than there are for Black artists in Canada.”

He told Gonez that the music business had left him discouraged about releasing records for a long time. An unpredictable music landscape and the industry’s darker side had worn him down.

Before his first record deal, Kardinal couldn’t always afford Toronto’s public transit. Other emerging artists helped him get by, pooling their money and personal connections.

He credited that community with helping him move forward, recalling how much artists had relied on one another when they lacked resources.

His career has since placed him on both sides of the business, as a recording artist and an executive involved in developing talent. He serves as Def Jam’s global A&R lead after previously working at Universal Music Canada. A&R departments are responsible for finding new artists and helping develop their recordings.

At Universal, he became the first Black senior vice president of A&R at a major Canadian label. He also established the Black Label Coalition, which raised money for charities during his tenure.

His work on access extends beyond a single label. Kardinal is a founding member of ADVANCE, Canada’s Black Music Business Collective, an organization supporting Black professionals across the country’s music industry.

ADVANCE’s work includes mentoring, advocacy and opportunities for people working throughout the business. That includes careers beyond performing, making its focus broader than helping an individual artist land a record deal.

As a performer, Kardinal’s 2001 album Quest for Fire: Firestarter, Vol. 1 helped introduce his Caribbean-influenced Toronto sound through records including “BaKardi Slang” and “Ol’ Time Killin’.”

For his latest record, he took an independent route. Firestarter Vol. 2: Everyday, Sometimes… is his first album since 2015’s Kardi Gras, Vol. 1: The Clash.

The new project brought together collaborators including Idris Elba, Buju Banton, Konshens, T-Pain and Melanie Fiona.

item.title: Khloe Kardashian Recounts Saving Naked Lamar Odom From 20 Hookers Holding Him Hostage
item.dc:creator: Nolan Strong
item.description: Khloe Kardashian says a chaotic hotel encounter during her marriage to Lamar Odom still shapes what she will not accept in dating.
item.content:encoded:
Khloe Kardashian says a chaotic hotel encounter during her marriage to Lamar Odom still drives her dating boundaries. She and Kris Jenner told the story on the November 5 episode of The Kardashians.

The memory came up during a truth-or-dare game with Kim Kardashian and her The Fifth Wheel co-stars. Jenner said the family got word that Odom was at a hotel during the height of his drug use.

She claimed they thought he was being held there against his will.

“We’re going to extract him from the situation because he’s being held hostage by these hookers,” Jenner recalled.

Kardashian said her security team entered the room first.

“And all I saw [was] they were literally having a circle jerk. There were 20 people in the room,” she said. She also said everyone was naked.

She said she rushed into the room and fought people. Jenner stayed in a bathroom and put drugs in trash bags. “I just lunge and start swinging, beating people up, and my mom is hiding in the bathroom,” Kardashian said on the show.

Kardashian framed the memory as a warning, not a reunion. She said the night still shapes the traits she will avoid in a man. She has also said she wants honesty and trust from any future partner.

The account adds detail to a marriage marked by public claims of infidelity and Odom’s substance use disorder. It is Kardashian and Jenner’s version of what happened that night.

Kardashian and Odom married in 2009. She filed for divorce in 2013. She withdrew the filing after Odom’s near-fatal 2015 overdose so she could help with his care. She filed again in 2016, and the divorce was final that December.

The two met on camera in 2025 after years apart. Their ties later broke down again. Kardashian said in April that their bridge was burned after she disputed parts of Odom’s Netflix film.

The Kardashians Season 8 is streaming on Hulu. New episodes arrive on Thursdays. People said Odom’s representative did not at once respond to a request for comment on this account.

item.title: RBX Appeals Spotify Bot-Streaming Lawsuit Dismissal
item.dc:creator: Mike Winslow
item.description: RBX has appealed the dismissal of his Spotify bot-streaming lawsuit after a federal judge ended the case with prejudice.
item.content:encoded:
RBX has taken his bot-streaming fight with Spotify to a federal appeals court, extending a case that a Los Angeles judge dismissed last month.

The Long Beach rapper filed an appeal after U.S. District Judge Josephine L. Staton ended his amended class-action lawsuit with prejudice. The federal docket lists a November 6 notice of appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit.

RBX, whose legal name is Eric Collins, sued Spotify in 2025.

He alleged that the streaming company allowed artificial plays to distort the royalty pool and reduce payments to independent artists. His complaint cited suspicious activity involving Drake’s catalog as one example. Spotify was the sole defendant.

The dispute moved through two versions of the complaint. Judge Staton dismissed the first version in June and gave RBX time to amend it.

He returned in July with broader allegations about selective enforcement of Spotify’s anti-fraud rules and the effect that bot activity could have on artists who rely on the same royalty pool.

The revised complaint still failed to clear the legal bar. In the October order, Judge Staton found that RBX had not pleaded enough facts to support his unfair-competition and negligence claims. She entered judgment for Spotify after dismissing the case with prejudice.

AllHipHop covered that ruling, which closed the case at the trial-court level. The new filing moves the fight to the Ninth Circuit, where RBX can challenge the legal reasoning behind the dismissal.

The appeal keeps a larger music-industry issue in view. Streaming services have tightened enforcement against artificial plays, while independent artists have questioned how platforms detect fraud and protect royalty pools.

RBX built his case around the argument that enforcement was uneven and harmed artists outside the biggest commercial catalogs.

The appellate court will review the record made before Judge Stanton.

RBX’s lawyers can argue that the complaint met the legal standard and that the case should return to the district court for more proceedings. Spotify will have a chance to defend the judgment.

The notice of appeal begins the next stage of the case. The Ninth Circuit will set the briefing schedule and decide whether to affirm the dismissal.
